talks.title: FIRST SIG Updates
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in FIRST SIG Updates.
talks.summary:
Overview: FIRST SIG leaders present updates at the Cyber Threat Intelligence Symposium, covering CVSS v4.0 development and other special interest group progress.

Key Topics: CVSS v4.0 finer granularity metrics and attack requirements; 3,000 person-hours of SIG effort; BTE (Base, Threat, Environmental) scoring model; public preview targeting December 2022; and other FIRST SIG initiatives.

Technical Details: Dave Dugal presents CVSS v4.0 improvements including enhanced user interaction metrics, attack requirements, and a bit.ly calculator preview for community feedback before NIST math finalization.

Takeaways: CVSS v4.0 addresses long-standing scoring granularity complaints. Security teams should review the preview calculator and provide feedback to shape the final specification.

talks.title: 0-day In-the-Wild Exploitation in 2022...so far.
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 0-day In-the-Wild Exploitation in 2022...so far..
talks.summary:
Project Zero’s Zero-Day Mission

Google Project Zero researcher Maddie Stone tracks zero-days exploited in the wild to drive structural mitigations and “make zero-day hard”—raising exploit cost and requiring more bugs per capability. She maintains public spreadsheets and a GitHub repository of in-the-wild zero-days since mid-2014.

2022 Statistics So Far

Through 2022 the team counted 18 in-the-wild zero-days. Nine were variants of previously patched bugs; four were variants of 2021 zero-days attackers reused within roughly twelve months because patches were incomplete. Stone argues this shows zero-days are not yet “hard.”

What “Hard” Would Look Like

Remote phone compromise via a link still typically chains about three zero-days (renderer RCE, sandbox escape, local privilege escalation). Harder ecosystems would require more chained bugs, novel bug classes, undocumented attack surfaces, non-reusable exploit techniques, and highly selective deployment rather than broad watering-hole burns.

talks.title: A Diamond is an Analysts Best Friend Introducing the Diamond Model for Influence Operations Analysis
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of A Diamond is an Analysts Best Friend Introducing the Diamond Model for Influence Operations Analysis.
talks.summary:
Defining Influence Operations

Recorded Future analyst Charity Wright opens a TLP:WHITE session distinguishing misinformation, disinformation, and fake news. Influence operations are organized attempts to change target-audience beliefs and decisions, often through propaganda and mass manipulation rather than kinetic effects alone.

Limits of Existing Frameworks

Prior analysis focused on content, voice, and dissemination but missed relationships among narratives, actors, and infrastructure. Kill chains like MITRE's disinformation chain and the AMITT TTP catalog help map adversary process yet lack psychosocial and geopolitical nuance, and new platforms outpace static TTP lists.

Narrative as the Core

Wright stresses that every campaign centers on a story. Humans assign meaning through narrative, especially stories invoking shared identity. Narrative warfare weaponizes those meanings to change behavior, an element often lost in technically focused CTI tradecraft.

The Adapted Diamond Model

Building on the 2013 intrusion Diamond Model, Wright's influence variant places narrative at the center. Technical axes retain capabilities and infrastructure; socio-political axes rename adversary to influencer and victim to audience, fusing essential campaign components for daily analysis of complex psychosocial threats.

talks.title: Attack Flow
talks.teaser: Beyond Atomic Behaviors examines Attack Flow.
talks.summary:
Beyond atomic behaviors

MITRE's Desiree Beck, Verizon's Gabriel Bassett, and Fujitsu's Ryu Masuka present Attack Flow, a Center for Threat-Informed Defense project. They argue CTI and incident response suffer when analysts treat isolated indicators as noise instead of recognizing related steps as a meaningful campaign sequence.

What an attack flow is

An attack flow models coordinated adversary behavior as structured objects and relationships rather than disconnected atomic events. Poor sequence understanding leads to weaker containment and remediation when campaigns unfold across multiple stages.

Graph representation with RDF

The data model builds on RDF triples—subject, predicate, object—mapped to source, relationship, and destination. This graph foundation supports reasoning across linked techniques, assets, and actions, with tooling aligned to semantic web standards for sharing and analysis at scale.
